A proposed ban on US diesel exports would upend the global market and boost shipping, according to Poten & Partners. Blocking exports of the fuel would eliminate above 20% of the 8m barrels per day moved daily across the globe, Poten tanker research head Erik Broekhuizen said.
It would send buyers in Europe and the rest of the Americas scrambling for diesel from India, Singapore, South Korea and maybe even China. A ban would also send refiners scrambling to export as many barrels as possible before it kicks in, he said.

Middle Eastern oil exports recover to highest level since Iran war began
28 September 2026 10:01
Crude oil exports from major Middle Eastern producers rebounded to 12.8 million barrels per day in September, reaching their highest level since the war started in February, according to preliminary data from analytics firm Kpler cited by Reuters .
According to Kpler’s estimates, oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz were set to reach around 7.4 million barrels per day in September. Following damage to the East-West pipeline in attacks, Saudi Arabia redirected part of its export flows from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Saudi oil exports are approaching 5.4 million barrels per day in September, compared with 2.446 million barrels per day in August. At the same time, shipments from the Ras Tanura port rose to around 3.6 million barrels per day, up from 929,000 barrels per day in August.
According to Kpler, 19 very large crude carriers (VLCCs) passed out of the Strait of Hormuz last week, each carrying around 2 million barrels of Saudi crude.
Despite the recovery in shipments, total oil exports from the region remain around 6 million barrels per day below their February level.

LONDON: Five vessels loaded with liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Ras Laffan, Qatar, are approaching the Strait of Hormuz, ship-tracking data showed on Saturday.
If the vessels successfully crossed the strait, it would be the first transit of LNG cargoes through the waterway since the US-Israel war with Iran began on February 28.
On Friday, Iran reopened the strait, which before the war carried a fifth of the world’s LNG trade, following a separate US-brokered ceasefire agreement on Thursday by Israel and Lebanon. A convoy of oil tankers was crossing the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday.
“Currently we see five laden vessels approaching the Strait of Hormuz. All five vessels loaded from Qatar’s Ras Laffan plant. Of the five, two are destined for Pakistan, two likely destined for India and one with no clear destination,” said Laura Page, manager of LNG Insight at Kpler.
“In addition, two ballast Adnoc vessels enter the Gulf of Oman and moor outside Fujairah. The vessel movements align with flaring data which suggests multiple trains at Ras Laffan’s north site have restarted as well as UAE’s Das Island plant,” she added.
Qatar is the world’s second-largest exporter of LNG, with shipments mostly going to buyers in Asia. Iranian attacks, however, knocked out 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG export capacity, with repairs expected to sideline 12.8 million metric tonnes per year of the fuel for three to five years.

Mitigation technologies can repel or intercept an unauthorized UAS. For example, interference signals can jam or break the communications connection between the UAS and its operator, which can trigger the UAS to land or return to its operator. According to the Bard College report, jamming is the most common mitigation technology.
Other mitigation technologies can use a net or kinetic force (such as lasers or projectiles) to disable or destroy the UAS. However, kinetic methods can be problematic because a falling or exploding UAS may cause unintended damage.
How mature is it?
Although the Department of Defense has used counter-UAS technology abroad since at least 2014, domestic use has been limited. Over the last 4 years, the authorized agencies have deployed some counter-UAS technologies domestically. Furthermore, few can successfully jam or disable a UAS, and many of those that can are only effective at around 1,000 feet or less.

The recent advisory from the U.S. Navy regarding naval mine threats in the Strait of Hormuz is not merely a routine safety warning. It is an admission of a blind spot.
For decades, the global economy has relied on the assumption that Western naval dominance ensures the free flow of oil through this narrow corridor. However, the Navy’s latest assessment reveals a sobering reality. We do not fully understand the scope, sophistication, or placement of underwater explosives in these waters.
The Blind Spot Beneath the Surface
Modern naval warfare often focuses on the spectacle of anti-ship missiles and drone swarms. These are visible, trackable, and frequently intercepted. Mines are different. Radiant is developing a 1.2MWe microreactor in shipping container as a portable microgrid power source which lasts 4-8 years depending on load. The product should be a viable alternative to the MEP-PU-810/A in use currently, which requires a continuous supply of ~4 tons of fuel per day at 75% load.
The reactor could be used as a resilient backup power, for remote fixed site power, or for expeditionary force use but it is not clear which of these use cases are viable for first unit deployment with an anchor customer.
Radiant desires to engage in studies of the logistics of these three use cases in detail, and to find locations and end users for the products along with high-level purchasing contacts at the AF.
Radiant will engage with all contacts to finalize the best approach to understanding the advantages, challenges, and customer requirements for microreactor fleet deployment scenarios. A detailed reactor model will be developed and delivered to AF staff to run advanced simulations for each scenario.

The Department of Defense (DOD) broke ground on the Project Pele transportable microreactor project at Idaho National Laboratory (INL).
The demonstration project is being led by DOD’s Strategic Capabilities Office and could be one of the first advanced reactors to operate in the United States as early as 2026.
Project Pele Breaks Ground
DOD is planning to design, build, and demonstrate a transportable high-temperature gas reactor that will operate at the lab’s Critical Infrastructure Test Range Complex.
The reactor will be manufactured by BWX Technologies and connected to INL’s microgrid producing 1 to 5 megawatts of electrical power.
Project Pele is a whole-of-government effort, with critical expertise provided by the Department of Energy, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, NASA, and the National Nuclear Security Administration.
The reactor is expected to operate for a minimum of three years at the lab and will help demonstrate the use of clean, reliable, and transportable nuclear power to help meet the increasing energy demands at military bases across the country.

Key Facts
* Reactors range from 1 MW to 20 MW and are contractor-owned and contractor-operated
* At least one reactor must be operational by September 30, 2028
The US Army selected five companies on August 26 to build nuclear microreactors at five installations. The agreements are worth up to $2.2 billion through fiscal 2031. The program is called Janus.
Fuel choices differ across the group. Radiant and Antares plan to use HALEU in TRISO form. General Atomics plans uranium zirconium hydride. Jeff Waksman, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment, leads the effort on the Army side.
The Army frames Janus as energy independence.
A 1 MW to 20 MW generator that runs for years without refueling is a microgrid asset, not a power plant. Diesel gensets and batteries carry most installations through an outage today. Both depend on fuel deliveries or on a short discharge window. A reactor sized to a base changes the resilience math, because the fuel is already on site.
They do not speed up the licensing.
Milestone-based payment protects the money, not the timeline. If Antares, BWXT, General Atomics, Radiant and Westinghouse all slip together, the Army has spent little and gained nothing on schedule. The resilience claim needs a test as well.
